name: Asian pears
tile_uses: Sliced raw, the salad, with cheese
why_now: California's Asian pear harvest runs from August into October, and the late varieties are the best of it. They're picked ripe and eaten crisp — unlike European pears, you don't wait for them to soften. They keep for weeks, which makes them October's lunchbox fruit.
how_to_choose: Firm all over; this pear is supposed to be hard
Russeted brown or smooth yellow, depending on the variety — both are good
No soft spots; they bruise easily, which is why they come in foam sleeves
buy_this_much: 3–4. Enough for the salad and a few afternoons.
price_note: Expensive in a supermarket, often half that at Asian markets in Convoy.

flavor_paths.name: Sliced cold
flavor_paths.description: Straight from the fridge. The default.

flavor_paths.name: In the salad
flavor_paths.description: Thin slices with arugula, walnuts, and pomegranate.

flavor_paths.name: With cheese
flavor_paths.description: Anywhere you'd use an apple. Juicier.

weekday_uses: Thin slices in the arugula salad
weekend_use: Sliced thin into the October salad, beside the whole fish.
storage: In the fridge, where they'll stay crisp for two or three weeks. Handle them gently; they bruise.
one_thing_to_learn: Some fruit is ripe when it softens, and some is ripe when it's picked. A European pear finishes ripening on your counter; an Asian pear is done when it comes off the tree, and waiting only makes it mealy. Knowing which is which saves a lot of fruit.
market_question: Which variety is this, and how long does it keep?
